source.title: Scaling Electronic Health Record Foundation Models for Population Health Management
source.authors: Li-Wen Sun; Hao-Ren Yao; O. Frieder; Xiang Qian; Chenyan Xiong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The scaling and benchmark figures are not available as extractable numerical data in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in structured electronic health records, a different modality and training setting from text language-model pretraining, and reports results on that setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation-loss IsoFLOP curves, fitted compute-optimal parameter and token scaling, architecture ablations, and downstream performance across model sizes. General benchmark comparisons and data-mixture results are not separate rows here unless they bear on a claim version. The paper also describes EHRSHOT task curves, but their individual numerical values are only in figures.
record.test_reason: The study fits IsoFLOP-based compute-optimal parameter and token power laws for decoder-only transformers pretrained on structured EHR code sequences, a non-text setting. It also reports downstream prediction at three model sizes, so its own results bear on V3, V5 and V6 in that setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say the fitted laws resemble Hoffmann et al.'s, although the exponents (0.34 vs 0.69) differ from equal growth. They further conclude that aligned cross-site data beats duplicating single-site data when data is limited. The scaling claim is limited to at most 2.4B parameters, with larger scales left open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses decoder-only transformers pretrained on aligned structured EHR code sequences and evaluates compute-optimal scaling and clinical prediction, rather than text language-model held-out loss scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports mild differences for tested architecture variants; it does not report sensitivity analyses of the fitted scaling exponents to fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: At 160m, the relative-position variant and the no-time-token variant change downstream breast-cancer AUROC by only 0.2–1.5 points; the authors call these mild differences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and input-representation details change downstream EHR performance only slightly at fixed size.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5: under the same token budget, 100M US tokens repeated 60x underperform a mixture of US tokens repeated 30x plus 3B NHIRD tokens on US downstream tasks (average 91.0/32.5/39.0 vs 91.2/33.4/40.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under data limits, adding aligned unique data beats repeating in-domain data, measured downstream rather than on loss.

record.code_released: The paper says code will be open-sourced and states in its checklist that source code will be released; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The scaling study covers limited model and compute ranges; the paper says it remains unclear whether trends continue at substantially larger scales. Numerical loss-curve values and EHRSHOT curve values are available only in figures. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the fitted scaling exponents.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 reports task-specific results for 11 diseases in each population and at several model sizes. Those individual task-by-model entries are not separately extracted; the average rows and the authors' explicit scale comparison are recorded instead. Figure 3 also contains task-specific EHRSHOT curves whose numerical values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: No text language-model loss is studied. Even for EHR, no power law of loss in N, D or C is fitted.
No fit on small runs is checked against much larger runs.
No depth/width or shape sweep evaluated on loss. Table 8 varies shape only together with size, and the ablations measure downstream metrics only.
Image and video, repeated-data scaling laws, and fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws are not tested. The power-law form of loss itself is not shown for EHR.
No comparison of fitting choices, parameter counting or schedules, and no report of curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Per-task scale trends are mixed: for example, NHIRD lung AUROC drops from 91.6 (160m) to 89.3 (1b), and US kidney sensitivity drops from 25.7 (1b) to 21.2 (2.4b). This matters when weighing the V6 averages.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The compute range is 1e18–2e20 FLOPs and Table 10 sizes run from 70m to 2.8b. The 2.4b downstream model is not among the Table 3 compute-optimal models, and its compute is unstated. The text's '5% sensitivity' gain for 2.4b over 160m holds only approximately (US +4.6, NHIRD +3.4). The divergent EHR allocation split is consistent with V7's data dependence, but the study does not itself vary fitting choices, so V7 is left untested.

versions.untested_parts: The paper profiles validation loss under IsoFLOP budgets, but does not report a fitted power law for loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute separately.
The study does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions against much larger runs.
Tests compute-optimal parameter and token scaling in EHR data; it does not test the original language-model setups or their fitting procedures.
Tests relative-position and time-token variations at 160m; it does not report a systematic sweep of depth and width.
Tests structured EHR pretraining only, not image or video models, repeated-data scaling as a general regime, fine-tuning scaling laws, or transfer scaling laws.
Reports downstream EHR prediction results at selected scales; it does not fit a general predictive relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance.
The study does not compare fitting choices or setups to establish how exponents depend on them, nor report curves bending away from a fitted power law.

relationships.reason: The token exponent (0.69) is about twice the parameter exponent (0.34), matching neither Kaplan's nor Hoffmann's split. The fits span only about two orders of compute and give no uncertainty (r2, r3).
